slides.0.title: Viticulture and climate
slides.0.subtitle: Viticultural challenges from frost, hail, rain and wind
slides.1.title: Spring frost and hail
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Frost in Cahors
slides.1.highlights.0.content: wein.plus reported temperatures of −4 to −6 °C on the night of 5–6 May, about 3,500 ha affected, 300 ha destroyed by April hail and roughly 60–70% of the expected crop lost (the article gives no year)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Repeated crop failures
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The same piece quotes the regional promotion head calling it the third crop failure in six years; the previous year's late frost had destroyed about 80% of the grapes
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Early budding in Jurançon
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Petit Manseng buds early, so March frost is a risk; training to about 2 m reduces ground-frost risk (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: Spring frost is the most direct yield risk in the South-West.
slides.2.title: Rain, humidity and wind
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Rainfall in Madiran
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Average temperature 12.5 °C and about 1,000 mm of rain, mostly in late winter and spring; a long dry autumn with occasional foehn is needed for full phenolic ripeness (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Morning mist at Monbazillac
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Cellar Tours: botrytis is aided by morning mists from the Gardonette tributary; Wine With Seth: a maritime climate with cold damp mornings and warm sunny afternoons
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Wind as a tool
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The Autan of Gaillac is a warm east wind; Jurançon's foehn dries the autumn and lets late-harvest grapes raisin on the vine
slides.2.content: Humidity helps at Monbazillac but Madiran needs a dry autumn.
slides.3.title: Density, varieties and drought
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Planting density
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Cahors requires at least 4,000 vines/ha (Wikipedia); Madiran historically had about 2,000, now at least 4,000, and top producers use 5,000–8,000 (wein.plus)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Tannat's roots
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Tannat's deep roots make it less dependent on drought stress and fertiliser, and new plantings use smaller-berried clones (wein.plus)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Vineyard management
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Yield restriction on older sites, blossom thinning, green harvesting, canopy work adapted to the season, and hand harvesting with pre-selection in the vineyard (wein.plus)
slides.3.content: Higher density and smaller berries aim at more concentrated ripeness.
slides.4.title: Old vines and conservation
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Plaimont's old vineyards
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Decanter: the Pédebernade vineyard at Sarragachies, from about 1830, was named France's first "vegetal" historical monument; Vignes Prephylloxériques is a half-hectare, almost all-Tannat plot planted in 1871
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Wild vines
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Wild vines (Vitis sylvestris) were found in hedgerows, and some think Petit Manseng is the cultivated vine genetically closest to them (Decanter)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Conservation and research
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Wine With Seth: Plaimont keeps a conservatory of old Tannat vines at Sarragachies (Gers); Decanter describes propagation from old vineyards and an annual two-day Rencontres Ampélographiques
slides.4.content: Old vines and rare varieties are living assets of the South-West.
